pull_request_body: Replace -X importtime with a sys.modules dump in the 56 startup-import probes. The budget check only needs the set of module names, which sys.modules provides at the end of the run. The -X importtime flag stays for the failure diagnostic: when a budget is breached, the probe re-runs with -X importtime to build the ten-slowest-imports message. All 56 probes, all four limits, and the control test are unchanged. The file takes at most half its present CPU time over three runs of pytest tests/commands/test_cli_startup_imports.py -n 0.
why: Issue #2369 reports that tests/commands/test_cli_startup_imports.py takes 204 s of the suite's 2,423 s. Each of its 56 probes starts a fresh interpreter under -X importtime, which adds per-import overhead to stderr and a Python parse of that text. The file is a structural budget and must stay, but its cost is the problem.
what_changes: Replace -X importtime with a sys.modules dump in the normal probe path
Add a timed re-probe that runs with -X importtime only when a budget fails
Keep all 56 probes, all four limits, and the control test unchanged
feasibility: The issue confirms the cost: 56 probes at about 4.2 s CPU each, with -X importtime adding per-import stderr lines and a Python parse. The file is at tests/commands/test_cli_startup_imports.py, and line 448 defines _probe_startup_imports.
sys.modules provides the set of loaded module names at the end of a run, which is all the budget count needs. The identifier matches confirm the four limit constants at lines 33-36 of the file.

First checks: run pytest tests/commands/test_cli_startup_imports.py -n 0 to get the baseline CPU time. Then run the same command after the change and confirm the total is at most half the baseline over three runs.
existing_tool: python -X importtime is the existing tool. It stays for the failure diagnostic message. The normal probe uses sys.modules, a Python built-in that requires no new dependency. No new tool is introduced.

added.name: startup-import-probe-mechanism
added.text: The startup-import probe SHALL collect the set of loaded module names via sys.modules in the normal path, and SHALL use -X importtime only in the failure diagnostic path to report the ten slowest imports by cumulative seconds.

scenarios.name: normal probe uses sys.modules
scenarios.when: a startup-import probe runs and the budget passes
scenarios.then: the probe collects module names from sys.modules without the -X importtime flag

scenarios.name: failure diagnostic uses importtime
scenarios.when: a startup-import probe runs and the budget fails
scenarios.then: the probe re-runs with -X importtime and the assertion message includes the ten slowest imports by cumulative seconds

groups.title: Replace -X importtime with sys.modules dump in the probe
groups.test: Write a test that asserts the subprocess args of _probe_startup_imports do not include -X importtime. The test mocks subprocess.run and checks the args list. Before the change, the args include -X importtime, so the test fails
groups.implementation: Modify _probe_startup_imports to build a -c script that imports the entry point, runs the command, then prints sorted(sys.modules.keys()) to stdout. Remove -X importtime from the subprocess args. Parse stdout instead of stderr for the module list

groups.title: Add timed re-probe for the failure diagnostic message
groups.test: Write a test that asserts _probe_startup_imports_timed exists and returns a list of (module, cumulative_seconds) pairs sorted by cumulative_seconds descending. Before the change, this function does not exist, so the test fails
groups.implementation: Add _probe_startup_imports_timed that runs the same argv with -X importtime and parses stderr for the ten slowest imports by cumulative seconds. Update the assertion helpers: when the module count exceeds the limit, call _probe_startup_imports_timed and include its result in the assertion message
